subject: Re: HarborBank onramp — VPC Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S (pilot decision)
messages:
From: Daria Novak <daria@harborbank.com>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 29 Jun 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Connectivity options for Redwood Private deployment (HarborBank pilot)

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — HarborBank is excited to move forward with a small pilot of Redwood Private for our internal fraud-detection models. Before we lock in an MLP, NetOps asked me to get a clear recommendation on access patterns. High level constraints:

- Regulated workload: no public egress for inference traffic; all traffic must traverse our monitored perimeter.
- Latency target: 40ms p95 or better from our primary DC in us-west-2.
- Throughput: sustained ~600 Mbps with short bursts up to 1.2 Gbps.
- We have overlapping RFC1918 ranges with some third-party tenants and cannot renumber without months of work.
- Must preserve source IPs so our logging and WAF can correlate traffic to internal services.
- Support multi-AZ resilience and a documented failover path.

Can you summarize the tradeoffs between cross-account VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and an IPsec site-to-site VPN for this pilot? Specific asks from NetOps: operational complexity, monitoring surface, NAT implications (SNAT/DNAT), and any compliance pitfalls.

Also loop in whoever owns the Private deployment networking runbook. We hope to decide this week.

Best,
Daria
NetOps — HarborBank
(eng-ops@harborbank.com)

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>

Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Connectivity options for Redwood Private deployment (HarborBank pilot)

Daria, thanks for the clear constraints — this is helpful. Quick summary up front, then specific tradeoffs below.

Recommendation (short):
- If you cannot renumber IP space, prefer AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) to avoid transitive routing and IP conflicts.
- If non-overlap can be guaranteed and you want lowest-latency, VPC Peering gives the simplest path (L3 routing, no additional NAT) but requires route table management and cross-account route approval.
- S2S VPN is the fallback for air-gapped sites or when you need BGP-based dynamic routing to on-prem gear, but it has higher and more variable latency and typically requires SNAT for scalable egress from Redwood's side.

Detailed tradeoffs:
1) VPC Peering
- Pros: Lowest per-packet overhead (no interface endpoints), direct routing (preserves source IPs end-to-end), predictable latency if in same region. No charge per-interface (regional data transfer costs still apply).
- Cons: Requires non-overlapping IPs, peering is not transitive (if you have multiple VPCs/regions you must peer each pair), route table scale and cross-account approvals add ops work. Cross-account IAM/acceptance can slow provisioning.
- Compliance note: Keeps traffic inside the cloud provider network, but you must prove isolation between tenants if auditors ask.

2) AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint)
- Pros: Works with overlapping IP space because traffic is tunneled to an endpoint ENI in your account; endpoint service model reduces blast radius and avoids route table pollution. Good for enforced isolation and least-privilege exposure.
- Cons: Preserves client source IP only up to the endpoint; the provider (Redwood) will see the endpoint ENI as the source unless we pass X-Forwarded-For-like headers at the application layer. There are ways to preserve original IPs (proxy protocol to the service), but that requires additional config and auditing for compliance. PrivateLink has per-GB charges and per-endpoint hourly costs.
- Compliance note: Strong isolation properties and good for regulated workloads, but you must document how source identity/logging is preserved.

3) Site-to-site VPN (IPsec)
- Pros: Works with any IP layout, supports BGP for dynamic failover, good for backhauls to on-prem appliances.
- Cons: Higher jitter and latency, usually needs a NAT gateway boundary depending on how provider side is implemented, and can complicate scaling (many tunnels to manage). Operational overhead for BGP session monitoring and rekeying.
- Compliance note: If you terminate in-house hardware, you get full control but must manage key rotation and auditing.

Operational asks / next steps:
- Ben: can you run a quick cost delta (per-month data + endpoints + NAT estimates) assuming 600Mbps sustained?
- Jordan: can you sketch an implementation checklist for both the PrivateLink path (endpoint service on Redwood, endpoint ENIs in HarborBank account) and the peering path (cross-account peering + route approvals + egress rules)?

I
m adding Ben and Jordan to help with runbook/ops detail. Happy to set up a 30-minute call with your NetOps team this week.

- Kimberly

Kimberly / Daria,

I ran a back-of-envelope cost + ops sketch. Attaching a small spreadsheet: connectivity_costs.xlsx (summary tab included). High-level findings:

- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): expected steady egress + endpoint cost for 600 Mbps sustained could be ~ $2.6k/month in us-west-2 assuming 4TB typical egress and the per-ENI hourly cost for two endpoints (multi-AZ) + provider-side service data charges. If we add proxy protocol or preserve client IPs via a TCP proxy layer, add ~ 2-3% CPU cost on the provider side under load.
- VPC Peering: avoids endpoint hourly charge and proxy overhead; raw data transfer costs slightly cheaper in-region. However, if HarborBank wants isolation per environment (prod/preprod) we will need multiple peering attachments which increases administrative effort.
- VPN (IPsec): cheaper on the provider-side for very low sustained egress volumes, but because of tunnel MTU/Jitter and rekeying, throughput efficiency drops; expect ~10-15% overhead (you may need bigger headroom). Also ops burden is higher: health checks, BGP flaps, and key rotation processes.

Operational notes:
- NAT implications: Peering preserves source IPs; PrivateLink will typically terminate at an ENI in HarborBank and we see ENI IPs unless we use proxy protocol. If HarborBank needs the original source IP in logs for compliance, we should confirm whether XFF/proxy is acceptable to their auditors.
- Monitoring: recommend Netflow + VPC Flow Logs + a dedicated endpoint health page in Redwood Console. We can emit trace-level spans for any requests routed via private endpoints to help troubleshooting.
- Resilience: For PrivateLink, recommend two endpoints in different AZs plus a DNS-based failover with short TTL. For peering, establish multi-AZ routing + pilot blackhole detection.

Attached: connectivity_costs.xlsx (spreadsheet).

If HarborBank cannot renumber and needs strong source-IP preservation without proxies, we should plan on a VPN termination at their aggregator appliance and pair that with an application-level token to maintain identity.

Happy to present numbers on the call.

Ben
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Quick implementation checklist and pilot plan (high-level):

1) PrivateLink pilot path (preferred if IP overlap persists)
   - Redwood creates a PrivateLink service (NLB fronting our provider-side service) and share the service name with HarborBank.
   - HarborBank creates interface endpoints (one per AZ) in their VPC that resolve to the ENIs.
   - Application layer: enable proxy-protocol v2 on the NLB and a lightweight TCP proxy (nginx/tcp-proxy) to preserve XFF/X-Proxy headers. We will log original source in an audit log shard for compliance.
   - Monitoring: VPC Flow Logs + CloudWatch metrics for endpoint ENIs + Redwood Console trace link.
   - Failover: DNS TTL 10s, TTL-based client retries, two endpoints across AZs.

2) VPC Peering pilot path (only if IPs are cleared)
   - Validate no overlapping prefixes; if overlap, require renumbering plan + maintenance window.
   - Create cross-account peering and propagate routes to relevant route tables; ensure no transitive exposure to other VPCs.
   - Security control: enforce SG rules to only allow the HarborBank CIDR blocks to Redwood subnets.
   - Monitoring: Route 53 health checks, metric alerts on route flaps, VPC Flow Logs.

3) VPN fallback path (for on-prem or heavy compliance needs)
   - Establish BGP session to customer CPE, monitor BGP state, and configure rekeying windows.
   - Use a NAT boundary if application requires it; document SNAT in audit runbook.

Proposed timetable:
- Tomorrow: 30-min alignment call with HarborBank NetOps to confirm IP overlap and source-IP logging requirements.
- Week+1: spin up PrivateLink service in Redwood staging and share service name for HarborBank to create endpoints.
- Week+2: end-to-end pilot traffic + SLO run (collect p95 latency and jitter).

Daria: can you confirm (1) whether auditors accept proxy-provided source headers as evidence, and (2) whether HarborBank can provision multi-AZ interface endpoints quickly?
